name: Waiting for a higher load round the clock
brief:
A data centre logs one load reading per hour slot of a day, and the same day repeats for ever. `load[i]` is the reading of slot `i`. For each slot, count how many slots forward you go to reach a strictly higher reading, wrapping from the last slot to the first. If no slot of the day reads higher, give `-1`.

Write `ring_waits(load)`, which returns the list of waits.

Example. For `load = [5, 3, 4, 1]` slot 0 holds the top reading, so it gives `-1`. Slot 1 waits 1 slot, and slot 2 wraps round to slot 0, 2 slots on. Slot 3 waits 1. The answer is `[-1, 1, 2, 1]`.
constraints: $0 \le n \le 200{,}000$ slots, each reading a whole number between $0$ and $10^9$.
$O(n)$ time is the target. Walking forward from every slot is too slow when many readings tie.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Walk the list twice, as if it were written out two days in a row. Keep a stack of slots still waiting; a higher reading pops every lower one and fixes its wait.

examples.note: Slot 2 wraps past the end to slot 0, so it waits 2.
A tie is not higher, so both slots give -1.

tests.call: (lambda w: (len(w), sum(w), w[:3], w[-3:]))(ring_waits([(i * 7919) % 100003 for i in range(200000)]))

how: Submit runs 13 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: Going round twice lets each slot see every other slot once, in the right order.
Only slots of the first pass are pushed, so no slot is given a wait of a full day or more.
Each slot is pushed once and popped at most once, so the work is $O(n)$.

planted.slip: It walks the day once, so a slot whose higher reading comes after the wrap stays at -1.
It pops on an equal reading, so a tie counts as higher.
It walks forward from every slot, which is $O(n^2)$ when the readings tie.
